content: Near drowning refers to a situation where an individual has come close to dying due to suffocation caused by submersion in water. Immediate first aid and medical attention are critical for anyone rescued from such an event. Symptoms of Near Drowning: The symptoms of near drowning can vary widely but may include the following: Swelling or distension of the abdomen. Bluish discoloration of the skin, particularly around the lips (cyanosis). Chest pain. Cold, pale skin. Confusion or disorientation. Coughing up pink, frothy sputum. Irritability or agitation. Extreme fatigue or lethargy. Absence of breathing. Restlessness. Shallow or gasping breaths. Loss of consciousness. Vomiting. Causes of Near Drowning: The causes of near drowning can include: Suicide attempts. Head trauma or seizures occurring while in the water. Alcohol consumption during swimming or boating. Falling through thin ice. Inability to swim or panic while swimming. Leaving young children unsupervised near bathtubs, pools, or other water sources. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: If you cannot safely rescue the drowning person without putting yourself at risk, immediately call for emergency medical assistance. If you are trained and capable of performing a rescue, do so and then call for medical help. All individuals who experience near drowning should be evaluated by a healthcare professional, even if they appear to recover quickly at the scene. Complications such as lung issues, fluid imbalances, or other traumatic injuries are common and may develop later. Treatment Options: When someone is drowning: Do not endanger yourself. Avoid entering the water or walking onto ice unless you are certain it is safe. Use a long pole, branch, or a throw rope attached to a buoyant object (e.g., a life ring or life jacket) to reach the person. Pull them to safety. If you are trained in water rescue, proceed only if you are confident it will not harm you. Be aware that individuals who have fallen through ice may be unable to grasp objects or hold on while being pulled to safety. If the person has stopped breathing, begin rescue breathing as soon as possible, even while still in the water. Continue rescue breaths every few seconds while moving the individual to dry land. Once on land, perform CPR if necessary. For detailed instructions on rescue breathing, refer to CPR guidelines. Exercise extreme caution when moving a drowning victim. Assume they may have a neck or spinal injury. Avoid bending or twisting their neck. Keep the head and neck stabilized during CPR and while moving the person. You can secure the neck with rolled towels or tape the head to a backboard or stretcher. Additional steps include: Administering first aid for any other serious injuries. Keeping the person calm and still while awaiting medical help. Removing wet, cold clothing and covering the individual with warm materials to prevent hypothermia. Reassuring the person, as they may cough or experience breathing difficulties once respiration resumes. What Not to Do: Do not attempt a swimming rescue unless you are trained in water rescue techniques. Avoid entering rough or turbulent water that could endanger you. Do not go onto ice to rescue someone unless you can safely reach them with an extended object. The Heimlich maneuver is not a routine part of near-drowning rescue. It should only be performed if repeated attempts to open the airway and provide rescue breaths have failed, and you suspect the airway is obstructed. Performing the Heimlich maneuver increases the risk of vomiting, which can lead to choking. Prevention: Avoid consuming alcohol while swimming or boating. Be aware that drowning can occur in any container of water. Do not leave standing water in basins, buckets, ice chests, kiddie pools, or bathtubs. Secure toilet seat covers with child safety devices. Fence all pools and spas. Install pool and door alarms and secure all doors leading outside. If a child is missing, check the pool immediately. Never allow children to swim alone or unsupervised, regardless of their swimming ability. Do not leave children unattended near any body of water, even for a brief moment. Many drownings occur when parents step away just for a minute. Follow water safety rules and consider taking a water safety course.
